blurb: The repos from the 16 October issue that we could write up, with what each one does and the setup steps from its own README.
intro: Issue #18 had five repos and no AI skills, and four of them have guides here. Most are for people who work with coding agents: XERJ gives your agent a local search index instead of grep, the plugin directory collects vetted Claude Code add-ons, and Ruflo runs teams of agents. Start with XERJ if your agent burns tokens reading files, or grab flipflop if you just want to send files between your own devices.

items.name: XERJ
items.cost: Free (Apache 2.0). Optional reranking through TypeSafe's Jev service needs your own key and is paid
items.works_with: Claude Code, Cursor, any MCP client, and any Elasticsearch client
items.short: A local search engine that indexes any folder so your coding agent pulls the exact passage it needs instead of reading whole files.
items.what: XERJ is a single binary that indexes code, docs, logs, PDFs, SQLite, CSVs and more with one command, and creates one index per dataset it finds. Code is parsed with tree-sitter, so results come back with symbols and `file:line`. It speaks the Elasticsearch API and also runs as an MCP server, and its main use is reference coding: your agent indexes similar open source repos and looks up how they solved a problem before writing code.
items.who: People whose agents spend a lot of tokens grepping and reading files, especially on private, internal or niche code. The README says it helps little or even hurts on popular public libraries the model already knows, so if that's most of your work, skip it.
needs: Linux, macOS or Windows on x86-64 or arm64
A stable Rust toolchain, only if you build from source

steps.title: Install it
steps.text: This downloads and runs the install script. On Windows PowerShell, use `irm https://xerj.org/get.ps1 | iex`. The installer prints where `xerj` landed, so add that to your PATH if needed.

steps.title: Start the server
steps.text: This is the local dev mode, with no TLS and no auth. Wait until `http://localhost:9200` responds.

steps.title: Wire it into your coding agent
steps.text: This sets up the MCP server and a skill for Claude Code or Cursor in one command.

steps.title: Search it
steps.text: You get ranked passages with `file:line`. `xerj def` jumps to a definition, and `xerj gain` shows what it saved you.
steps.code: xerj search "how do we rotate the WAL segment"

steps.title: Connect another MCP client
steps.text: Run the node from step 2 first. Add an `xerj` entry to your MCP client's config with the absolute path to the binary (usually `~/.local/bin/xerj`), the argument `mcp`, and `XERJ_URL` set to `http://localhost:9200`. `xerj mcp --help` prints the full config block.

try.label: From the README
try.text: "Run `xerj autoindex map` and tell me what is in this data (types, counts and the gotchas it recorded), then answer my questions with search instead of reading files."

watch: The install command pipes a download straight into your shell. Read the script first.

`--insecure` turns off TLS and API key auth, so anything that can reach the port can read and delete every index. The README says it's meant for one user on a dev machine, and a fresh node binds only to `127.0.0.1`. On a shared host, start without `--insecure` and use the key in `<data-dir>/admin.key`.
Optional reranking sends the text of your top results to TypeSafe's servers. It stays off until you set a key, and `[rerank] enabled = false` blocks it completely.
The default embedder is lexical and works offline. The neural embedder is opt-in and downloads about 90 MB.
The project asks users to send back a short field report as a pull request. That's optional.

items.name: Claude Code Plugins Directory
items.short: Anthropic's curated marketplace of Claude Code plugins, which you can browse and install from inside Claude Code.
items.what: This repo is a plugin marketplace for Claude Code. Plugins in `/plugins` are built and maintained by Anthropic, and the ones in `/external_plugins` come from partners and the community. A plugin can bundle slash commands, agents, skills and MCP server settings.
items.who: Claude Code users who want vetted add-ons in one place. If you use another coding agent, it won't help you, since the install runs through Claude Code's plugin system.

steps.title: Browse the directory
steps.text: Inside Claude Code, open `/plugin` and go to Discover to look through what's available.

steps.title: Install a plugin by name
steps.text: Replace `{plugin-name}` with the plugin you picked.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Open `/plugin`, go to Discover, and install one plugin that fits your work.

watch: The README tells you to trust a plugin before you install, update or use it. Anthropic says it doesn't control the MCP servers, files or other software inside plugins and can't verify that they work as intended or won't change.
Third-party plugins live in `/external_plugins`. Check each plugin's homepage before installing one.

items.name: Ruflo
items.works_with: Claude Code, Codex and other clients that support MCP
items.short: A harness around Claude Code and Codex that adds agent swarms, memory across sessions and a console to watch runs and costs.
items.what: Ruflo, formerly Claude Flow, wraps your coding agent with extra agents, swarm coordination, memory and hooks. The full CLI install adds 98 agents, 60+ commands, 30 skills, an MCP server, hooks and a daemon to your project. A lighter path installs only the Claude Code plugins you choose, and a console shows workflows, agents, tokens and cost.
items.who: People who already work daily in Claude Code or Codex and want several agents coordinating on bigger jobs. It changes a lot about how your agent behaves, so if you want a simple setup, try a single plugin first or skip it.
needs: Claude Code 2.1.287 or later for the plugin path
`npx`, for the CLI install and the MCP server
On Windows, Git-Bash, WSL or MSYS for the one-line installer, or use the `npx` command instead

steps.title: Add the marketplace in Claude Code
steps.text: Run these inside Claude Code. This is the lite path, with no files written to your workspace.

steps.title: Install core, the console and mods
steps.code:
/plugin install ruflo-core@ruflo
/plugin install ruflo-console@ruflo
/plugin install ruflo-mods@ruflo
/reload-plugins

steps.title: Or do the full install in your project
steps.text: The setup wizard runs the same on every platform. It adds `.claude/`, `.claude-flow/`, `CLAUDE.md`, helpers and settings to your project.

steps.title: Connect another MCP client
steps.text: For Codex or another client with local stdio MCP servers, set the command to `npx` with the arguments `["-y", "ruflo@latest", "mcp", "start"]`. The equivalent command is below.

try.label: From the README
try.where: The Ruflo console in Claude Code
try.text: In `/ruflo`, set Settings, Claude control to write + ask, then ask: "Create a mission to add a dark mode toggle. Show me the mission and its status." Approve the create action when it asks.

watch: Mods run with your account's permissions and aren't sandboxed. The README says to read their code before installing.
The full CLI install writes files and hooks into your project, and the hooks route tasks in the background.
Console control lets the AI run console actions. The default is read + ask. Network, spending and destructive actions still need your confirmation in auto mode.
The README also offers `curl -fsSL https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ruvnet/ruflo@main/scripts/install.sh | bash`. That pipes a download straight into your shell, so read the script first.
Federation lets your agents exchange work with agents on other machines. The README says PII is stripped before anything leaves your node.

items.name: flipflop
items.short: Pairs your devices once, then lets any of them send files, links or text to the others over Bluetooth, LAN or the internet.
items.what: flipflop sets up a trusted tunnel between two or more devices. After that, one device can send files to another at any time, nearby or far away. It's built on Iroh.
items.who: Anyone who moves files, links or notes between their own devices, or a family's devices. There's no iOS build, so iPhone users can't use it.
needs: A Linux, macOS, Windows or Android device on each end
For building from source: Rust with `cargo`, and for Android, `just`, `cargo-apk`, the Android SDK and NDK

steps.title: Download a build
steps.text: Get the latest Linux, macOS or Windows build or the Android APK from the releases page at github.com/andunieee/flipflop/releases/latest. On Windows, run the executable directly or use the `-setup.exe` installer.

steps.title: Or build it yourself
steps.text: The first line builds the desktop app and the second installs on Android.
steps.code:
cargo run --release          # desktop
just android-install         # Android (needs cargo-apk, Android SDK + NDK)

try.label: From the README
try.text: Set up a tunnel between your laptop and your phone, then send a link or some plain text from one to the other.

watch: Windows shows a "Windows protected your PC" warning when you run it, according to the README.
The README is short and doesn't explain pairing or security in detail, so expect to work some things out in the app.
